# Calibration study of uncertainty parameters for nearly-zero energy buildings based on a novel approximate Bayesian approach. The calibration process began with the identification of key uncertain parameters in a nearly-zero energy building (NZEB) through global sensitivity analysis. Therefore, this study presents a novel and effective method for building energy consumption calibration, offering significant practical value. The common calibration methods for building energy models include model-based methods, optimization-based methods, and Bayesian calibration methods [18]. To reduce computation time, some researchers have incorporated machine learning models into the Bayesian calibration framework [26], using surrogate models to replace building energy simulation software for calculations. [27] employed a GP proxy model for Bayesian calibration of a building energy model incorporating user information at different resolutions, significantly reducing simulation time. Although the introduction of the MCMC method and machine learning models enables Bayesian calibration to obtain the posterior distribution of uncertain parameters in the shortest possible time, the prerequisite for performing Bayesian calibration is knowing the prior distribution of the parameters and the likelihood function. Section 2 introduces the sensitivity analysis method, the data-driven machine learning model construction approach, the adopted ABC calibration method, and its performance evaluation index. First, the uncertainty parameters and their prior distributions were determined based on existing research and expert experience, followed by the use of EnergyPlus to establish a baseline model for building energy consumption simulation. ### Model calibration for building energy efficiency simulation. ### Calibrating whole building energy models: detailed case study using hourly measured data. ### Influences of energy data on Bayesian calibration of building energy model. ### Guidelines for the Bayesian calibration of building energy models. ### Bayesian calibration of building energy models with large datasets. ### A Bayesian approach with urban-scale energy model to calibrate building energy consumption for space heating: a case study of application in Beijing. ### Review on building energy model calibration by Bayesian inference. * ### Toward high-fidelity nearly-zero energy building models: a multi-stage calibration framework using optimization algorithm and sub-hourly field data. The proposed method calibrated uncertainty parameters and trained rapid predictive models, significantly enhancing the accuracy and explainability of multi-objective optimization results for building retrofits.

Title: Bayesian calibration of hyperelastic constitutive models of soft tissue - ScienceDirect
## Article preview. ## Journal of the Mechanical Behavior of Biomedical Materials. # Research paper Bayesian calibration of hyperelastic constitutive models of soft tissue. Constitutive models of soft tissue mechanical response are widely used in biomedical and biomechanical applications ranging from traumatic brain injury simulation to computer-aided surgery and functional tissue engineering. In the case of soft tissue constitutive models, aleatory uncertainty is associated with the parameters in the model arising from noise in the experimental observations, and epistemic uncertainty is associated with the choice of a particular constitutive model. This is also sometimes referred to as model form uncertainty (Oberkampf et al., 2004). We propose a Bayesian calibration framework based on Nested Monte Carlo Sampling technique for soft tissue constitutive models in which the aleatory uncertainties are properly addressed. The Bayesian method for calibration is gaining interest in a wide range of science and engineering areas, from seismology (Bui-Thanh et al., 2013) to atmospheric dispersion modeling (Keats et al., 2010). The parameters are estimated using the Delayed Rejection Adaptive Metropolis (DRAM) MCMC algorithm. We also highlight the importance of taking into account the multimodal nature of the likelihood functions arising in these problems, which means local approaches like the quadratic approximation of the posterior can lead to erroneous results. Even if a global optimum is found, it may not result in a physically admissible parameter set. For the latter, we use the function lsqcurvefit (based on the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm) in the software (MATLAB, 2013), as well as the material modeling tool in the finite element software ABAQUS (Abaqus 6.12 Theory Manual, 2012). ### J. ### J. ### J. ### Med. results.title: Comparing frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty quantification in two‐step constitutive model calibration - Tröger - 2024 - PAMM - Wiley Online Library
results.content: # Comparing frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty quantification in two-step constitutive model calibration. In this study, we perform two-step statistical parameter inference for an elasto-plastic constitutive model utilizing a frequentist approach and Bayesian inference. The uncertainties are quantified by different methods, in particular, we compare an asymptotic normality analysis and Gaussian error propagation in the frequentist setting with sampling-based Bayesian inference. Although frequentist and Bayesian parameter inference differ significantly in the way parameters are calibrated, both methods yield similar estimates. However, the uncertainties of the elasticity parameters in the frequentist approach are found to be significantly smaller compared to Bayesian inference, due to the underlying approximations in the frequentist setting. In order to obtain reliable simulation results, these models must undergo calibration employing experimental data, commonly referred to as model calibration or material parameter identification. While constitutive model calibration is a common task, the quantification of material parameter uncertainties is often overlooked during calibration. In this work, we present a comparative study of model calibration and uncertainty quantification utilizing both frequentist and Bayesian inference, where a special focus lies on multistep identification procedures. Subsequently, a two-step calibration of an elasto-plastic constitutive model is performed including a thorough examination of the identified material parameters and their associated uncertainties. However, in multistep model calibrations, which are common in constitutive model calibration, uncertainty quantification is more delicate since the uncertainty of previously identified parameters has to be considered. Note that the Gaussian error propagation requires sensitivities between material parameters, which is in contrast to the multistep uncertainty quantification using asymptotic normality, where the sensitivity of the model response with respect to the uncertain parameters is required. The two methods discussed, frequentist model calibration and Bayesian inference, will be compared in terms of the obtained parameter values and the corresponding uncertainties. Results from model calibration and uncertainty quantification utilizing frequentist approach and Bayesian inference. In contrast to the frequentist approach discussed above, a sampling-based Bayesian approach can be used to identify the material parameters and to quantify uncertainties. The same calibration procedure as in the frequentist setting is performed: first, the elasticity parameters are calibrated, then a Monte-Carlo approach is employed to calculate , and, finally, the plasticity parameters are identified.

results.title: A probabilistic approach with built-in uncertainty quantification for the calibration of a superelastic constitutive model from full-field strain data - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: A probabilistic approach with built-in uncertainty quantification for the calibration of a superelastic constitutive model from full-field strain data - ScienceDirect
## Computational Materials Science. Volume 192, May 2021, 110357. # A probabilistic approach with built-in uncertainty quantification for the calibration of a superelastic constitutive model from full-field strain data. Author links open overlay panel, , , , ,. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.commatsci.2021.110357Get rights and content. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Abstract. We implement an approach using Bayesian inference and machine learning to calibrate the material parameters of a constitutive model for the superelastic deformation of NiTi shape memory alloy. We use a diamond-shaped specimen geometry that is suited to calibrate both tensile and compressive material parameters from a single test. We adopt the Bayesian inference calibration scheme to take full-field surface strain measurements obtained using digital image correlation together with global load data as an input for calibration. The calibration is performed by comparing these two experimental quantities of interest with the corresponding results from a simulation library built with the superelastic forward finite element model. We present a machine learning based approach to enrich the simulation library using a surrogate model. This improves the calibration accuracy to the extent permitted by the accuracy of the underlying material model and also improves the computational efficiency. We demonstrate, verify, and partially validate the calibration results through various examples. We also demonstrate how the uncertainty in the calibrated superelastic material parameters can propagate to a subsequent simulation of fatigue loading. This approach is versatile and can be used to calibrate other models of superelastic deformation from data obtained using various modalities. This probabilistic calibration approach can become an integral part of a framework to assess and communicate the credibility of simulations performed in the design of superelastic NiTi articles such as medical devices. The knowledge obtained from this calibration approach is most effective when the limitations of the underlying model and the suitability of the training data used to calibrate the model are understood and communicated. ## Graphical abstract. ## Keywords. ## Cited by (0).
